solution:
a. 'A' is terylene (also called dacron), the polyester of section 15.3.6. Ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid undergo condensation polymerization, an alcoholic \(\mathrm{-OH}\) of the glycol condensing with a \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) of the acid and eliminating water to give an ester link :

\(n\,\mathrm{HO-CH_2-CH_2-OH} + n\,\mathrm{HOOC-C_6H_4-COOH} \xrightarrow[-n\mathrm{H_2O}]{533\ \mathrm{K},\ \Delta} \mathrm{[O-CH_2-CH_2-O-CO-C_6H_4-CO]_n}\)

b. 'B' is nylon 6,6, the polyamide of section 15.3.5. Hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid first form the nylon salt, which on condensation polymerization at high temperature and pressure loses water and gives the amide link \(\mathrm{-CO-NH-}\) :

\(n\,\mathrm{H_2N-(CH_2)_6-NH_2} + n\,\mathrm{HOOC-(CH_2)_4-COOH} \xrightarrow[-n\mathrm{H_2O}]{533\ \mathrm{K}} \mathrm{[CO-(CH_2)_4-CO-NH-(CH_2)_6-NH]_n}\)

[Textbook misprint: two spelling slips, both preserved as printed. Part b writes "Novolak", while the chapter's own Fig. 15.3 and section 15.3.7 spell it "Novolac" - and item (iv) of the MCQ block on this SAME printed page uses the "Novolac" spelling, so the book contradicts itself within one page. Part d writes "addtion" for addition. Neither affects the answers.]

a. Caprolactam is used to prepare **nylon 6**. Section 15.3.5 shows \(\varepsilon\)-caprolactam heated with water at 533-543 K undergoing ring opening polymerization to \(\mathrm{[NH-(CH_2)_5-CO]_n}\).

b. Novolak is a copolymer of **phenol** \((\mathrm{C_6H_5OH})\) **and formaldehyde** \((\mathrm{HCHO})\). Section 15.3.7 forms it in the first two stages of bakelite manufacture, phenol and formaldehyde reacting over an acid or base catalyst.

c. Terylene is a **condensation** polymer of terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol (section 15.3.6), water being eliminated as each ester link forms.

d. Benzoyl peroxide used in addition polymerisation acts as an **initiator (catalyst) that generates free radicals**. Section 15.2.3 names it in the chain initiation step, alongside acetyl peroxide and tert-butyl peroxide.

e. Polyethene consists of polymerised **ethylene (ethene) units**, \(\mathrm{[CH_2-CH_2]_n}\) (section 15.3.2).

Section 15.2.3 gives three modes of polymerization, and this branch of the tree diagram of Fig. 15.2 is :

Polymers (based on mode of polymerization)

|-- Addition polymerization (chain growth) - monomers with a double bond add on with NO loss of a small molecule; e.g. polythene, PVC, polyacrylonitrile.

|-- Condensation polymerization (step growth) - polyfunctional monomers join with elimination of a small molecule such as \(\mathrm{H_2O}\), \(\mathrm{HCl}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3OH}\) or \(\mathrm{NH_3}\); e.g. terylene, nylon 6,6, bakelite.

|-- Ring opening polymerization - a cyclic monomer (lactam, cyclic ether, lactone) opens and adds one unit at a time; e.g. \(\varepsilon\)-caprolactam giving nylon 6.

Addition polymers (formed from monomers containing a double bond, with no small molecule lost) : polythene, PVC (from vinyl chloride), polyacrylonitrile (from acrylonitrile), teflon (from tetrafluoroethylene), natural rubber or polyisoprene, neoprene and Buna-S.

Condensation polymers (formed from polyfunctional monomers with elimination of a small molecule) : terylene or dacron, nylon 6,6, bakelite (phenol-formaldehyde), melamine-formaldehyde resin and urea-formaldehyde resin.

Section 15.2.3 gives addition polymerization the alternative name chain growth polymerization, so the chain growth polymers are the addition polymers of this chapter : polythene (LDP and HDP), polyacrylonitrile (orlon), teflon or polytetrafluoroethylene, PVC, natural rubber (polyisoprene), neoprene and Buna-S.

1) Monomer : the small molecule from which the repeating units of a polymer are derived. Section 15.1 defines polymers as giant macromolecules made from repeating units derived from small molecules called monomers.

2) Vulcanisation : the process by which a network of cross links is introduced into an elastomer (section 15.3.1). Raw rubber is heated with sulfur powder in presence of accelerators at about \(150\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\); the sulfur cross links the polyisoprene chains and improves tensile strength, stiffness, elasticity and toughness.

3) Synthetic fibres : man made polymeric solids that form threads. Section 15.2.1 places fibres among the synthetic polymers, and section 15.2.4 defines fibres as polymeric solids which form threads, possessing high tensile strength because of strong intermolecular forces such as hydrogen bonding and dipole-dipole attraction; e.g. nylon 6,6 and terylene.

Weak **van der Waals forces** of attraction. Section 15.3.2 states that high density polythene is essentially a linear polymer whose high density arises from close packing, and Problem 15.2 states that polythene chains carry only weak van der Waals forces as their intermolecular interaction. Because the chains are linear and unbranched they can lie close together, so these short range van der Waals forces act effectively along the whole chain and pull the chains into a closely packed, crystalline arrangement of high density. In low density polythene the chains carry branches, which keep them apart and loosely held, and the density is correspondingly low.

Copolymer : Buna-S, which section 15.2.5 gives as an example because it is formed from two different monomers, butadiene and styrene, whose repeating units are randomly sequenced in the chain. (Buna-N is a second example.)

Homopolymer : polythene, which has only one type of repeating unit and is formed from the single monomer ethylene. (Polypropene, nylon 6 and polyacrylonitrile are further examples from the same section.)

Thermoplastic : 1. PET and 3. Polythene. Section 15.2.4 defines thermoplastic polymers as those capable of repeated softening on heating and hardening on cooling, with moderately strong intermolecular forces, and names polythene among them; section 15.3.6 calls PET the most common thermoplastic.

Thermosetting : 2. Urea formaldehyde resin and 4. Phenol formaldehyde. The same section defines thermosetting polymers as rigid polymers that harden while hot, become infusible and cannot be remoulded because of extensive cross linking by covalent bonds, and names bakelite (phenol formaldehyde) and urea formaldehyde resin as its examples.

Section 15.2.4 classifies polymers into four classes on the basis of intermolecular forces.

1. Elastomers : the intermolecular forces are the weakest of the four, of the van der Waals type, so the chains can be stretched apart by an external force. A few cross links between the chains pull the stretched polymer back to its original shape when the force is removed, which is what makes the material elastic. Examples : vulcanised rubber, Buna-S, Buna-N, neoprene.

2. Fibres : the intermolecular forces are the strongest of the four - hydrogen bonding and strong dipole-dipole attraction. These hold the chains closely and regularly, so the solid is crystalline and has high tensile strength, that is resistance to breaking under tension, and can be drawn into threads. Examples : polyamides such as nylon 6,6, polyesters such as terylene.

3. Thermoplastic polymers : the intermolecular forces are moderately strong, intermediate between those of elastomers and fibres, and there is no cross linking. The chains therefore slide past one another on heating and lock again on cooling, so the polymer softens repeatedly on heating and hardens on cooling and can be moulded again and again. Examples : polythene, polystyrene, polyvinyls.

4. Thermosetting polymers : here the chains are joined by extensive cross linking through covalent bonds formed in the mould during the hot setting process, giving a rigid three dimensional network. Once hardened the polymer is infusible and cannot be softened or remoulded. Examples : bakelite, urea formaldehyde resin.

a. Nylon 6 (section 15.3.5) - ring opening polymerization of \(\varepsilon\)-caprolactam, a cyclic amide, on heating with water :

\(n\,(\varepsilon\text{-caprolactam}) \xrightarrow[533-543\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{H_2O}} \mathrm{[NH-(CH_2)_5-CO]_n}\)

The seven membered lactam ring, \(\mathrm{-NH-CO-(CH_2)_5-}\), opens at the amide bond and one monomer unit at a time adds to the growing chain, so the repeating unit has the same elemental composition as the monomer.

b. Terylene (section 15.3.6) - condensation polymerization of ethylene glycol with terephthalic acid over a zinc acetate-antimony trioxide catalyst at 420-460 K, eliminating water at each ester link :

\(n\,\mathrm{HO-CH_2-CH_2-OH} + n\,\mathrm{HOOC-C_6H_4-COOH} \xrightarrow[-n\mathrm{H_2O}]{420-460\ \mathrm{K}} \mathrm{[O-CH_2-CH_2-O-CO-C_6H_4-CO]_n}\)

[Textbook misprint: the stem prints "thier" for "their". Preserved as printed; the question is unambiguous.]

Natural rubber (section 15.3.1)

Monomer : isoprene, that is 2-methyl-1,3-butadiene, \(\mathrm{CH_2{=}C(CH_3)-CH{=}CH_2}\).

Polymer : natural rubber is a high molecular mass linear polymer of isoprene, that is cis-polyisoprene, with the repeating unit

\(\mathrm{-[CH_2-C(CH_3){=}CH-CH_2]_n-}\)

The chapter notes that the \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\) double bond in the polyisoprene molecule has the cis configuration, which gives the chain its coiled shape and leaves only weak van der Waals forces between chains.

Neoprene rubber (section 15.3.9)

Monomer : chloroprene, that is 2-chloro-1,3-butadiene, \(\mathrm{CH_2{=}C(Cl)-CH{=}CH_2}\).

Polymer : neoprene is the addition polymer of chloroprene, with the repeating unit

\(\mathrm{-[CH_2-C(Cl){=}CH-CH_2]_n-}\)

Both are addition polymers of a conjugated diene and both retain one double bond per repeating unit, which is what allows them to be vulcanised.

The linkage \(\mathrm{-C(=O)-O-}\) is the **ester linkage**, so the polymer is a **polyester**. Section 15.3.6 states that the polyester polymers have an ester linkage joining the repeating units, and section 15.2.3 shows the link being formed when an alcoholic \(\mathrm{-OH}\) group condenses with a \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) group and a water molecule is eliminated. Terylene (dacron) and PET are the chapter's examples; polycarbonates are also described there as a kind of polyester polymer.

a. SBR rubber, that is Buna-S, the copolymer of 1,3-butadiene (75 parts) with styrene (25 parts) from section 15.3.8 and Fig. 15.5 :

\(\mathrm{{\sim}CH_2-CH{=}CH-CH_2-CH_2-CH{=}CH-CH_2-CH_2-CH(C_6H_5)-CH_2-CH{=}CH-CH_2{\sim}}\)

The butadiene and styrene units are randomly sequenced along the chain, which is why it is a copolymer.

b. Buna-N rubber, the copolymer of butadiene with acrylonitrile listed in Table 15.1 :

\(\mathrm{[H_2C-CH{=}CH-CH_2-CH_2-CH(CN)]_n}\)

c. Neoprene rubber, the addition polymer of chloroprene from section 15.3.9 :

\(\mathrm{[CH_2-C(Cl){=}CH-CH_2]_n}\)

[Textbook misprint: two defects in the printed pair-list, both preserved. The monomer for polyester is printed "polyhydoxyglycol", a dropped r in polyhydroxyglycol. And the labelling of the right-hand column changes style part way down: items 1 and 2 are labelled "a." and "b." with a full stop, while items 3, 4 and 5 are labelled "c)", "d)" and "e)" with a closing bracket. Neither affects the matching.]

| Name of polymer | Monomer |
|---|---|
| 1. Teflon | b) \(\mathrm{CF_2{=}CF_2}\) |
| 2. PVC | c) \(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CHCl}\) |
| 3. Polyester | e) Dicarboxylic acid and polyhydoxyglycol |
| 4. Polythene | a) \(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2}\) |
| 5. Bakelite | d) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH}\) and \(\mathrm{HCHO}\) |

Section 15.3.3 gives tetrafluoroethylene \(\mathrm{(CF_2{=}CF_2)}\) as the monomer of teflon; Table 15.1 gives vinyl chloride \(\mathrm{(CH_2{=}CHCl)}\) for PVC and ethylene \(\mathrm{(CH_2{=}CH_2)}\) is the monomer of polythene in section 15.3.2; section 15.3.6 makes the polyester terylene from a dicarboxylic acid (terephthalic acid) and a glycol (ethylene glycol); and section 15.3.7 makes bakelite from phenol and formaldehyde.

1. Adipic acid + hexamethylenediamine give **nylon 6,6** (section 15.3.5). The \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) group of the acid condenses with the \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) group of the diamine, eliminating water and forming the amide link, so the polymer is

\(\mathrm{[CO-(CH_2)_4-CO-NH-(CH_2)_6-NH]_n}\)

The numerals 6,6 stand for the six carbon atoms in each of the two bifunctional monomers.

2. \(\varepsilon\)-Aminocaproic acid + glycine give **nylon 2-nylon 6** (section 15.5.2), the biodegradable polyamide copolymer of the two amino acids. Condensation of the \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) of one amino acid with the \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) of the next, with loss of water, gives

\(\mathrm{[NH-CH_2-CO-NH-(CH_2)_5-CO]_n}\)

in which the \(\mathrm{NH-CH_2-CO}\) unit comes from glycine (2 carbon atoms) and the \(\mathrm{NH-(CH_2)_5-CO}\) unit from \(\varepsilon\)-aminocaproic acid (6 carbon atoms), which is the origin of the numbers 2 and 6 in the name.

The repeating unit of natural rubber is the **isoprene unit**, so natural rubber is cis-1,4-polyisoprene. Its structure is

\(\mathrm{-[CH_2-C(CH_3){=}CH-CH_2]_n-}\)

Section 15.3.1 states that the monomer is isoprene, 2-methyl-1,3-butadiene, that natural rubber is a high molecular mass linear polymer of isoprene, and that the \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\) double bond in the polyisoprene molecule has the cis configuration. The chain therefore carries a methyl branch and one double bond in every four carbon atoms; the number of such units varies from about 2000 to 5000, giving molecular masses from 130,000 u to 340,000 u.

[Textbook misprint: two spelling slips in the list of polymers to classify, both preserved as printed - item g reads "Polyacrylonitrle" for polyacrylonitrile (spelt correctly in section 15.3.4) and item h reads "Phenol-formedehyde" for phenol-formaldehyde (spelt correctly in section 15.3.7). Neither affects the classification.]

Natural polymers (obtained from plant or animal sources, section 15.2.1) : a. Cellulose, d. Starch, e. Protein.

Synthetic polymers (man made, prepared by polymerization or copolymerization of monomers) : b. Polystyrene, c. Terylene, f. Silicones, g. Orlon (polyacrylonitrile), h. Phenol-formaldehyde resins.

Cellulose is the plant polymer of cotton and wood pulp named in sections 15.2.1 and 15.3.10; starch and protein are the natural biopolymers section 15.1 refers back to. Terylene is the polyester of section 15.3.6, orlon the polyacrylonitrile fibre of section 15.3.4, phenol-formaldehyde resin the bakelite of section 15.3.7, and polystyrene appears as the thermocol polymer in Table 15.1. Silicones are not discussed in this chapter, but they are man made polymers and the chapter's Activity section asks the student to look them up; they are therefore synthetic.

[Textbook note (not an error): this question asks the student to name some NATURAL resins, and the chapter names none. It nowhere defines the word "resin" either; it uses the term only in the compound names of three synthetic thermosetting polymers (phenol-formaldehyde, urea-formaldehyde and melamine-formaldehyde resins) and in calling polycarbonates high melting thermosetting resins. That half of the question therefore cannot be answered from this chapter's own text, and the model answer says so rather than supplying an outside fact.]

Synthetic resins are man made polymers, generally cross linked condensation products of simple monomers, which are supplied as a mouldable powder or a viscous liquid and are then set in a mould into a hard, rigid, infusible article. In this chapter they are the thermosetting polymers of section 15.2.4, whose extensive covalent cross linking makes them infusible and impossible to remould once hardened.

Synthetic resins named in this chapter : phenol-formaldehyde resin, that is bakelite, with novolac as its intermediate moulding powder (section 15.3.7 a); melamine-formaldehyde resin (section 15.3.7 b); and urea-formaldehyde resin (section 15.2.4 and Table 15.1). Polycarbonates are described in section 15.3.6 as high melting thermosetting resins.

Natural resins : the chapter names none. It nowhere defines the word "resin" and gives no example of a natural resin, so that part of the question cannot be answered from this chapter's own text.

| Thermosetting resins | Thermoplastic resins |
|---|---|
| Rigid polymers with extensive cross linking by covalent bonds. | Linear or lightly branched chains with no cross linking. |
| Shaped on heating during formation, but they harden while still hot. | Soften repeatedly on heating and harden again on cooling. |
| Once hardened they become infusible and cannot be softened by heating, so they cannot be remoulded. | Can be softened and remoulded again and again. |
| Cross links are formed in the mould during the hot hardening or setting process. | Held only by moderately strong intermolecular forces, intermediate between those of elastomers and fibres. |
| Examples : bakelite, urea formaldehyde resin, melamine formaldehyde resin. | Examples : polythene, polystyrene, polyvinyls, PET. |

Both definitions are those of section 15.2.4, which classifies polymers by their intermolecular forces.

Bakelite is made from two raw materials (section 15.3.7 a) :

1. Phenol, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH}\)

2. Formaldehyde, \(\mathrm{HCHO}\) (also written \(\mathrm{CH_2O}\))

The two react in presence of an acid or base catalyst to give the moulding powder novolac, which on further heating at \(138\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) to \(176\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) under high pressure cross links to the thermosetting polymer bakelite.
